historical_timeline.summary: Born in Geneva; his mother dies nine days later.
Almost continual retention of urine in his early years, by his own account.
Writes of urinary retention, at 36; later treats himself with Daran's bougies for eight or ten years.
Frequent retentions with a rupture; a year of languor.
A probe breaks in his urethra.
Asks in his will that his body be opened after death.
Stones thrown at his house at Môtiers.
Settles at Wootton, Staffordshire, and begins the Confessions.
Becomes convinced that the man who arranged his stay in England is plotting against him; the two quarrel violently.
Leaves Wootton and flees to France.
Writes the Dialogues and tries to leave the manuscript at Notre-Dame.
Writes the Reveries of the Solitary Walker.
Dies suddenly at Ermenonville; apoplexy certified; the autopsy finds no urinary lesion.

claims.statement: Jean-Jacques Rousseau was born in Geneva on June 28, 1712. Geneva had followed the Gregorian calendar since 1701, so the date needs no conversion.

source_links.locator: Geneva's council resolved on December 31, 1700, to follow the new calendar

claims.statement: His mother, Suzanne Bernard, died nine days after his birth.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The 1911 Britannica says she died in childbirth; no cause beyond the birth is recorded.

claims.statement: In the Confessions he wrote that a defect in the bladder caused him an almost continual retention of urine in his early years; that he reached thirty almost without feeling this original infirmity, apart from frequent heats in the bladder; that burning and pain in the loins returned at Venice; and that after a hot summer of journeys on foot he had a violent nephritic colic, after which he never recovered his former health.
claims.clinical_interpretation: His own account. Nephritic colic is an eighteenth-century term for severe loin pain, not a modern diagnosis.

claims.statement: In the Confessions he wrote that the surgeon Morand advised him to go to Daran, whose bougies were the only ones that gave him any relief; he bought a great number of them so that he would never be without, and used them often for eight or ten years.
claims.clinical_interpretation: His own account of self-treatment with urethral bougies.

claims.statement: His letters show that he spoke of urinary retention from 1748, at 36. In 1761 a probe broke in his urethra and he feared it would cost him his life; he wrote that he could not stop using his probes for a single day and that he had carried a bladder disease since childhood. A surgeon, Brother Côme, succeeded in passing a probe and ruled out a stone.
claims.clinical_interpretation: His own letters as quoted in a 2023 history-of-medicine paper. The same paper reports that he thought of suicide after the 1761 accident; this record notes that only as past history and gives no detail.

claims.statement: He described his trouble as a habitual state: he never passed urine with a full stream, the flow was never wholly stopped, and he judged that the stream grew thinner from year to year and would one day stop altogether.
claims.clinical_interpretation: His own description as quoted in a 2023 history-of-medicine paper.

claims.statement: In 1758 he suffered frequent retentions together with a rupture, and passed the year in a state of languor that made him think he was near the end of his life.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Rupture was the term of the time for a hernia; the site is not stated.

claims.statement: In a will dated January 29, 1763, he asked that his body be opened after death, to show that his urinary disorder did not come from a dissolute life.
By his own account in the Confessions he had five children with Thérèse Levasseur, and all five were taken to the foundling hospital shortly after birth.
claims.clinical_interpretation: His own account. The 1911 Britannica records a later doubt that the children existed. No health facts about the children are recorded here.

claims.statement: His books were condemned in 1762; stones were thrown at his house at Môtiers in September 1765; and he came to England in January 1766 at the invitation of a Scottish philosopher. He lived at Wootton, in the parish of Ellastone in rural Staffordshire, from March 22, 1766, to May 1, 1767, in a house belonging to Richard Davenport, and wrote the first part of the Confessions there.

source_links.locator: Page 92: the condemnation of Emile in 1762

claims.statement: In England he became wrongly convinced that the Scottish philosopher who had arranged his stay was at the center of a plot against him, and he feared that the servants were spying on him. The two men quarreled violently, and the 1911 Britannica called his letters of this time those of a lunatic.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Documented conduct and beliefs; calling them a delusion is interpretation (see CLM-0015).

claims.statement: In May 1767 he fled from England to France, and he later lived in France for a time under the name Renou.

From 1772 he wrote the Dialogues (Rousseau, Judge of Jean-Jacques), a work born of his sense of persecution and long read as evidence of growing paranoia; he meant to leave the manuscript on the high altar of Notre-Dame in Paris but found the chancel fenced off by a locked railing.

His last work, the Reveries of the Solitary Walker (written 1776 to 1778), opens: "Me voici donc seul sur la terre" (So here I am, alone on earth), and says he has been in this strange position for more than fifteen years.

The French psychiatrists Sérieux and Capgras classed him among patients with a delusion of interpretation, and a 2023 history-of-medicine paper judges that by current criteria he had a paranoid delusion that appeared around the age of 45 and grew afterwards, while noting that he had real enemies and real persecution (his books condemned, and expulsion by the Swiss authorities).
claims.clinical_interpretation: Retrospective interpretation; no diagnosis was made in his lifetime, and real persecution makes the line between belief and delusion hard to draw.

claims.statement: The cause of his urinary disorder is disputed. Proposed causes include a congenital narrowing of the urethra (Poncet and Leriche, and his own phrase, a defect of conformation), a stricture of the penile urethra (judged most probable in a 2023 paper), a muscular valve at the bladder neck (Mercier), urinary retention of psychological origin (Janet), and acute intermittent porphyria (Androutsos and Geroulanos, 2000).
claims.clinical_interpretation: Retrospective diagnoses that disagree with one another and with the autopsy (CLM-0017).

claims.statement: The autopsy done the day after his death found no stone and no lesion of the kidneys, ureters, bladder, or urethra.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The report of the surgeon who opened the body, quoted in a 2000 urology history paper; later writers questioned its methods.

claims.statement: He died suddenly at Ermenonville on July 2, 1778, less than two months after moving to the estate of the Marquis de Girardin; a local inquiry the next day certified death from apoplexy. Rumors of suicide circulated, but an examination of his skull in 1897 found no trace of a bullet wound.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Apoplexy is an eighteenth-century term; the exact cause is not known.

claims.statement: He distrusted the medicine of his time: in Emile he wrote that he would never call a physician for himself unless his life were in evident danger, and in the Confessions he wrote that the physicians he consulted gave him no relief and weakened him.
In a letter he wrote that when snow and frost shut him in he split wood to make himself sweat twice a day, the only remedy that had ever given him the least relief.
claims.clinical_interpretation: His own words as quoted in a 2023 history-of-medicine paper; the letter is not dated there.

synthetic_episode.teaching_objective: Assess a 54-year-old writer with long-held beliefs that former friends are plotting against him, poor sleep, and lifelong difficulty passing urine. Engage him without arguing with or endorsing the beliefs; exclude medical, substance, and neurocognitive causes; distinguish delusional disorder, persecutory type, from paranoid personality disorder, schizophrenia, and a mood disorder with psychotic features (DSM-5-TR); assess the risk of harm to himself and to others at every visit; offer cognitive behavioral therapy for psychosis and an antipsychotic by shared decision-making, accepting a refusal and offering again; and, if he starts one, choose a drug with little anticholinergic effect and follow the metabolic monitoring schedule. In parallel, evaluate chronic incomplete emptying with uroflowmetry, post-void residual, kidney function and ultrasound, retrograde urethrography, and cystoscopy; stop self-dilation; and offer urethroplasty instead of further dilation for a stricture that has recurred for decades (AUA 2023), with his capacity to consent assessed, not assumed absent because of the delusional beliefs. The teaching note contrasts this with his documented lifelong self-treatment with bougies and the disputed causes of his illness.

hpi.narrative: Mr. Rousseau returns two weeks after presenting with long-held beliefs of a plot against him, poor sleep, and difficulty passing urine. He saw Dr. Lindqvist-Hale of psychiatry this morning. The kidney and bladder ultrasound eleven days ago showed normal kidneys without hydronephrosis and a thickened, trabeculated bladder. Five days ago the urology team performed a retrograde urethrogram, a voiding cystourethrogram, and a flexible cystoscopy: a dense, ring-like narrowing 1.5 cm long in the proximal bulbar urethra, with a lumen of about 8 French, which the scope could not pass; the meatus is normal, with no hypospadias, and the bladder neck opens normally. He has not used his urethral sounds since the first visit, as advised; his stream is no worse and he has not been unable to pass urine. He read the reports himself and brought written questions. He still sleeps about four hours and spends much of the day thinking about the people he believes are working against him, and he has stopped opening letters from people he suspects. He has had no thoughts of suicide or of harming anyone and has made no plan to confront anyone.

assessment.assessment: Non-bizarre persecutory delusions for well over a month (about nine years), with function preserved apart from the effects of the beliefs, and no hallucinations, disorganization, or negative symptoms, so the criteria for schizophrenia are not met. Paranoid personality disorder describes pervasive suspicious attitudes held as attitudes; his beliefs are fixed, specific, and unshaken by contrary evidence, which makes them delusions, although long-standing sensitive and suspicious traits may have preceded them. The mild depressive and anxious symptoms followed the beliefs and are not a mood episode with psychotic features. A normal neurological examination, MoCA 28, normal laboratory tests, no substance use, and a long, stable course make a medical or neurocognitive cause unlikely, so brain imaging is not needed now; it would be if cognition declined, neurological signs appeared, or the course changed. The beliefs grew from real conflicts, which should be acknowledged rather than dismissed

Low risk of suicide and of violence at present: no current ideation, no history of violence, no wish to confront anyone, no weapons, and no substance misuse. The risks to watch are sudden flight from his home, isolation, insomnia, and any shift toward wanting to confront someone. Outpatient care is safe

An antipsychotic often reduces the distress and preoccupation of delusional disorder, though the beliefs may persist. Aripiprazole 5 mg is the best choice for him: it has almost no anticholinergic effect, so it will not worsen urinary retention, and it causes little sedation, weight gain, or prolactin rise. Drugs with marked anticholinergic effects, such as olanzapine, quetiapine, or the low-potency first-generation drugs, should be avoided. I offered it framed around his own goals of sleep and peace of mind; he declined today, which he is entitled to do, and it should be offered again

He is suitable for cognitive behavioral therapy for psychosis aimed at distress, worry, sleep, and safety behaviors rather than at the truth of the beliefs. He accepted it. Engagement depends on not arguing with or colluding in the beliefs, acknowledging his real grievances, keeping promises, and letting him read his records

He understands and retains information about his urinary condition and its treatment, appreciates that it applies to him, weighs the options, and communicates a choice.
